hook_text: The soil under your shoes took longer to make than any building in your town, and one storm can wash it away.
clip_script: Look down. That dark layer of soil took hundreds of years to form, a centimetre at a time. Plants guard it. Leaves soften the rain. Roots hold it together like a net. Now pull the plants away. A heavy storm hits bare ground. First the water strips off a thin sheet of soil. Then it cuts little channels. Then the channels become dongas, gullies deeper than a house. Farming that leaves soil bare does this. So do building sites, where bulldozers scrape the land clean. So do mines and their bare dumps. The soil washes into rivers and fills up dams with mud. In a dry country, that is water we cannot store. Once the topsoil is gone, it does not come back in our lifetime.
visual_style: A close-up of dark topsoil and roots; raindrops splashing on bare earth; brown runoff cutting rills; an aerial view of a deep donga in green hills; a bulldozer on a building site; a pale mine dump with dust blowing; a dam with a muddy delta at its inflow.
pacing: Slow at the soil, faster as the water cuts deeper, then a quiet ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn how people speed up soil erosion and why it matters.
